title: Game of Thrones Text Analysis
text:
The Dataset
The game-of-thrones.csv dataset contains the complete scripts from all seasons of the HBO television series.
Dataset Structure:

Date: Original air date of each episode
Season: Season number (1-8)
Episode: Episode number within each season
Title: Episode title
Name: Character name
Sentence: The dialogue spoken in the episode

title: Game of Thrones Text Analysis
text:
Analysis Methodology
Both analyses uses a “tidy text” approach, where raw dialogue is tokenized into individual words, processed to remove noise, and then aggregated for insights. Multiple sentiment lexicons are compared to provide a nuanced view of emotional content.

title: Game of Thrones Text Analysis
text:
Navigation

Frequency Analysis: Explore the most frequent words, characters, and topics in Game of Thrones dialogue
Sentiment Analysis: Discover how emotional tone evolves across seasons and episodes

title: Sentiment Analysis
text:
Sentiment analysis examines the emotional tone of text. Rather than just counting words, sentiment analysis assigns emotional values to words and aggregates them to understand the overall emotional trajectory.
This analysis uses these three approaches:

Dictionary Comparison: Comparing multiple sentiment lexicons to understand nuances
Sentiment Trajectory: Tracking how sentiment evolves across the series
Contribution Analysis: Identifying which words have the greatest impact on sentiment



Code
library(tidyverse)
library(tidytext)
library(plotly)

got <- read_csv("game-of-thrones.csv")
bing <- read_csv("bing.csv")
nrc <- read_csv("nrc.csv")

got_tokens <- got %>%
  unnest_tokens(word, Sentence)

got_tokens <- got_tokens %>%
  group_by(Season, Episode) %>%
  mutate(episode_id = cur_group_id()) %>%
  ungroup()

title: Sentiment Analysis
section: Part 1: Dictionary Comparison - Bing vs NRC
text:
Part 1: Dictionary Comparison - Bing vs NRC
Different sentiment lexicons capture emotion in different ways. Bing provides binary sentiment (positive/negative), while NRC provides multiple emotion categories (joy, fear, anger, anticipation, etc.).

Plot 1: Binary Sentiment Comparison (Bing Lexicon)
The Bing lexicon classifies words as either positive or negative.


Code
bing_sentiment <- got_tokens %>%
  inner_join(bing, by = "word") %>%
  count(Season, sentiment) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = sentiment, values_from = n, values_fill = 0) %>%
  mutate(net_sentiment = positive - negative,
         Season = as.factor(Season))

bing_plot <- bing_sentiment %>%
  pivot_longer(cols = c(positive, negative), names_to = "sentiment", values_to = "count") %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = Season, y = count, fill = sentiment)) +
  geom_col(position = "dodge") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("positive" = "green", "negative" = "red")) +
  labs(title = "Positive vs Negative Words by Season", x = "Season", y = "Word Count", fill = "Sentiment") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 12))

ggplotly(bing_plot, tooltip = c("x", "y", "fill"))








Plot 2: Emotion Categories (NRC Lexicon)
The NRC lexicon provides a richer emotional picture by categorizing words into specific emotions beyond just positive/negative.


Code
nrc_sentiment <- got_tokens %>%
  inner_join(nrc, by = "word") %>%
  count(Season, sentiment) %>%
  mutate(Season = as.factor(Season))

nrc_plot <- nrc_sentiment %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = Season, y = n, fill = sentiment)) +
  geom_col() +
  facet_wrap(~sentiment, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_fill_viridis_d() +
  labs(title = "Emotion Distribution by Season", x = "Season", y = "Word Count", fill = "Emotion") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 12), legend.position = "bottom", strip.text = element_text(face = "bold", size = 9))

ggplotly(nrc_plot, tooltip = c("x", "y", "fill"))








Lexicon Comparison Summary

Bing Lexicon reveals an overall balance between positive and negative sentiment across the series, with notable variation by season.
NRC Lexicon shows that emotions like positive, negative, trust are most prevalent in Game of Thrones dialogue, reflecting the show’s dramatic and often dark narrative.

title: Sentiment Analysis
text:
Part 2: Sentiment Trajectory
How does emotional tone shift throughout the series?

Plot 3: Net Sentiment Over Time (by Episode)
This visualization tracks the cumulative sentiment trajectory across all episodes.


Code
sentiment_trajectory <- got_tokens %>%
  inner_join(bing, by = "word") %>%
  mutate(sentiment_value = ifelse(sentiment == "positive", 1, -1)) %>%
  group_by(Season, Episode, episode_id) %>%
  summarise(net_sentiment = sum(sentiment_value), total_words = n(), sentiment_score = net_sentiment / total_words, .groups = 'drop') %>%
  arrange(Season, Episode) %>%
  mutate(episode_num = row_number())

trajectory_plot <- sentiment_trajectory %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = episode_num, y = sentiment_score, color = as.factor(Season), group = 1)) +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5, size = 2) +
  geom_smooth(se = TRUE, color = "black", alpha = 0.1, method = "loess", span = 0.3) +
  scale_color_viridis_d(name = "Season") +
  labs(title = "Sentiment Score Trajectory Across All Episodes", x = "Episode Number (Chronological)", y = "Sentiment Score (positive - negative) / total words", color = "Season") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 12))

ggplotly(trajectory_plot, tooltip = c("x", "y", "color"))


`geom_smooth()` using formula = 'y ~ x'








Plot 4: Average Sentiment by Season
Which seasons are emotionally the most intense?


Code
season_sentiment <- sentiment_trajectory %>%
  group_by(Season) %>%
  summarise(avg_sentiment = mean(sentiment_score), min_sentiment = min(sentiment_score), max_sentiment = max(sentiment_score), .groups = 'drop') %>%
  mutate(Season = as.factor(Season))

season_plot <- season_sentiment %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = Season, y = avg_sentiment, fill = avg_sentiment)) +
  geom_col(show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = min_sentiment, ymax = max_sentiment), width = 0.3, alpha = 0.6) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = "red", mid = "gray", high = "green", midpoint = 0) +
  labs(title = "Average Sentiment Score by Season", subtitle = "Error bars show min-max range", x = "Season", y = "Average Sentiment Score") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 12), plot.subtitle = element_text(face = "italic",  size = 10))

ggplotly(season_plot, tooltip = c("x", "y"))

title: Sentiment Analysis
text:
Part 3: Contribution Analysis
Which specific words contribute the most to the overall sentiment?

Plot 5: Top Positive Word Contributions
Words with the highest positive contribution (frequency × positive sentiment value).


Code
positive_contributions <- got_tokens %>%
  inner_join(bing, by = "word") %>%
  filter(sentiment == "positive") %>%
  count(word, sort = TRUE) %>%
  head(15) %>%
  mutate(word = reorder(word, n),
         contribution = n)

positive_plot <- positive_contributions %>%
  ggplot(aes(contribution, word, fill = contribution)) +
  geom_col(show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = "lightgreen", high = "darkgreen") +
  labs(title = "Top 15 Positive Words Contribution",
       x = "Frequency",
       y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 12))

ggplotly(positive_plot, tooltip = c("x", "y"))








Plot 6: Top Negative Word Contributions
Words with the highest negative contribution (frequency × negative sentiment value).


Code
negative_contributions <- got_tokens %>%
  inner_join(bing, by = "word") %>%
  filter(sentiment == "negative") %>%
  count(word, sort = TRUE) %>%
  head(15) %>%
  mutate(word = reorder(word, n),
         contribution = n)

negative_plot <- negative_contributions %>%
  ggplot(aes(contribution, word, fill = contribution)) +
  geom_col(show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = "lightcoral", high = "darkred") +
  labs(title = "Top 15 Negative Words Contribution",
       x = "Frequency",
       y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 12))

ggplotly(negative_plot, tooltip = c("x", "y"))

title: Frequency Analysis
text:
Frequency analysis shows the most important topics in a text by examining word occurrence patterns. After removing common stop words (the, and, of, etc.), we can identify which topic dominate the Game of Thrones dialogue.


Code
library(tidyverse)
library(tidytext)
library(plotly)

got <- read_csv("game-of-thrones.csv")

got_tokens <- got %>%
  unnest_tokens(word, Sentence) %>%
  anti_join(stop_words)

got_tokens <- got_tokens %>%
  mutate(Season = as.factor(Season))

title: Frequency Analysis
text:

title: Frequency Analysis
text:
Plot 1: Most Common Words Overall (Interactive)
The most frequently occurring words in the entire series provide a high-level summary of the dominant themes and concepts in Game of Thrones dialogue.


Code
top_words_plot <- got_tokens %>%
  count(word, sort = TRUE) %>%
  head(20) %>%
  mutate(word = reorder(word, n)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(n, word, fill = n)) +
  geom_col(show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = "steelblue", high = "darkblue") +
  labs(title = "Top 20 Most Frequent Words in Game of Thrones", 
       x = "Frequency Count", 
       y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 12))

ggplotly(top_words_plot, tooltip = c("x", "y"))

title: Frequency Analysis
section: Plot 2: Word Frequency Trends by Season
text:
Plot 2: Word Frequency Trends by Season
How do the most common themes shift as the series progresses?


Code
top_10_words <- got_tokens %>%
  count(word, sort = TRUE) %>%
  head(10) %>%
  pull(word)

season_trends <- got_tokens %>%
  filter(word %in% top_10_words) %>%
  count(Season, word) %>%
  ggplot(aes(Season, n, color = word, group = word)) +
  geom_line(size = 1) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  labs(title = "Top 10 Words: Frequency Trends Across Seasons", x = "Season", y = "Frequency", color = "Word") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 12), legend.position = "right")

ggplotly(season_trends, tooltip = c("x", "y", "color"))

title: Frequency Analysis
text:
Plot 3: Most Frequent Characters Speaking
Who speaks the most in Game of Thrones?

  count(Name, sort = TRUE) %>%
  head(15) %>%
  mutate(Name = reorder(Name, n)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(n, Name, fill = n)) +
  geom_col(show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = "coral", high = "darkred") +
  labs(title = "Top 15 Characters by Number of Sentences Spoken", x = "Number of Sentences", y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal() +

ggplotly(character_freq, tooltip = c("x", "y"))

title: Frequency Analysis
section: Plot 4: Top Words Used by Top Characters
text:
Plot 4: Top Words Used by Top Characters
What words are most commonly spoken by the major characters?


Code
top_characters <- got %>%
  count(Name, sort = TRUE) %>%
  head(5) %>%
  pull(Name)

character_words <- got_tokens %>%
  filter(Name %in% top_characters) %>%
  count(Name, word, sort = TRUE) %>%
  group_by(Name) %>%
  top_n(8, n) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  mutate(word = reorder_within(word, n, Name)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(n, word, fill = Name)) +
  geom_col(show.legend = TRUE) +
  facet_wrap(~Name, scales = "free") +
  scale_y_reordered() +
  labs(title = "Most Common Words by Top 5 Characters", x = "Frequency", y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 12), strip.text = element_text(face = "bold"))

ggplotly(character_words, tooltip = c("x", "y"))

title: Frequency Analysis
text:
Plot 5: Vocabulary Richness by Season
How diverse is the vocabulary in each season? A larger vocabulary might indicate more varied dialogue.


Code
vocab_diversity <- got_tokens %>%
  group_by(Season) %>%
  summarise(unique_words = n_distinct(word),
            total_words = n(),
            avg_word_length = mean(nchar(word))) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = Season, y = unique_words, fill = Season)) +
  geom_col(show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_line(aes(group = 1), color = "black", size = 0.8) +
  scale_fill_viridis_d() +
  labs(title = "Vocabulary Diversity by Season",
       subtitle = "Number of Unique Words Used",
       x = "Season",
       y = "Number of Unique Words") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 12),
        axis.text.x = element_text(size = 10))

ggplotly(vocab_diversity, tooltip = c("x", "y"))

title: Frequency Analysis
section: Plot 6: TF-IDF Analysis - Words Distinctive to Each Season
text:
Plot 6: TF-IDF Analysis - Words Distinctive to Each Season
TF-IDF (Term Frequency-Inverse Document Frequency) identifies words that are uniquely important to each season. High TF-IDF scores indicate words that appear frequently in one season but rarely in others.


Code
tfidf_data <- got_tokens %>%
  count(Season, word, sort = TRUE) %>%
  bind_tf_idf(word, Season, n) %>%
  group_by(Season) %>%
  top_n(8, tf_idf) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  mutate(word = reorder_within(word, tf_idf, Season))

tfidf_plot <- tfidf_data %>%
  ggplot(aes(tf_idf, word, fill = Season)) +
  geom_col(show.legend = TRUE) +
  facet_wrap(~Season, scales = "free") +
  scale_y_reordered() +
  scale_fill_viridis_d() +
  labs(title = "Most Distinctive Words by Season (TF-IDF Analysis)",
       x = "TF-IDF Score",
       y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 12),
        strip.text = element_text(face = "bold"))

ggplotly(tfidf_plot, tooltip = c("x", "y", "fill"))

title: Frequency Analysis
text:
Summary of Key Findings
The frequency analysis reveals:

Dominant Themes: Words like “lord,” “king,” and “know” dominate the dialogue, reflecting the show’s focus on politics, power, and relationships.
Character Focus: A small group of characters dominates the dialogue, with Jon Snow, Daenerys, and Tyrion among the most frequently speaking characters.
Vocabulary Consistency: The series maintains relatively consistent vocabulary richness across seasons, suggesting sustained narrative complexity.
Seasonal Variation: Certain seasons emphasize particular themes—identifying distinctive words shows how plot focuses shift throughout the series.

title: Sentiment Analysis
text:
Summary

The Bing lexicon captures a binary view of sentiment, which is useful for quick assessment. NRC provides emotional granularity that reveals specific emotional tones shown in the series.
The series shows a most upward but mixed trajectory, withthe first season being most negative and last season being most positive.
The sentiment is driven primarily by recurring words that appear throughout the series, such as “good”, “well”, “right” for positive sentiment and “stark”, “dead”, “kill” for negative sentiment.

text:
Summary

Words like “lord,” “king,” and “father” dominate the dialogue, which matches the show’s focus on power and relationships.
A small group of characters dominates the dialogue, with Jon Snow, Daenerys, and Tyrion among the most frequently speaking characters.
